claims.text: Increasing compressive strain in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs alters the local electronic environment.
The strain-induced electronic change shifts adsorption free energies of oxygenated ethanol intermediates toward optimal values.
PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
Single-metal catalysts generally promote no more than a four-electron ethanol oxidation process.
Compressive strain promotes the 12-electron ethanol oxidation pathway over the four-electron pathway.
The proposed initial PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles are uniform, well mixed, and have minimal pre-existing strain.
Synthesis or post-synthesis treatment can controllably increase compressive strain while leaving catalyst composition constant.
Compressive strain modifies surface atomic spacing.
Compressive strain modifies the local surface electronic density.
The strained catalyst surface has a Gaussian-like distribution of adsorption free energies for key oxygenated intermediates.
Heterogeneous neighboring active sites in high-entropy alloys can possess different local electronic structures that enable selectivity tuning in complex reactions.
Strain perturbation of ligand and strain effects generates both strongly and weakly binding active sites.
The proposed distribution of binding strengths facilitates intermediate adsorption and activation.
The proposed distribution of binding strengths facilitates C-C bond cleavage and subsequent oxidation required for the 12-electron pathway.
Relative to a low-strain baseline, the strained catalyst will have greater selectivity toward CO2 or other fully oxidized products.
Relative to a low-strain baseline, the strained catalyst will have greater catalytic activity because of optimized intermediate adsorption energetics.
The proposed effect applies where intermediate adsorption and electron transfer are rate-limiting.
Extreme temperature or pH can fundamentally alter the ethanol oxidation mechanism and therefore invalidate the proposed strain effect.
X-ray diffraction or TEM lattice measurements can characterize the relevant nanoscale surface strain.
In situ infrared or X-ray absorption spectroscopy can determine adsorption free energies of the key intermediates.
